## Compute (wall − startup; the `startup` row is wall)

**Columns run fastest → slowest** — generated from each table's score row, so the header order
always matches the data. **Bold** = Brood. The suite is split into separate tables because not
every row compares the same thing: one 7-column table would let a data-structure choice or a
native library read as a runtime result.

### Like-for-like — same algorithm, same data structures

Every language expresses these the same way, so the ordering is a runtime comparison.

In `vs best` / `vs avg`, **`+` is slower, `−` is faster**. Rank and distance often disagree:
`nqueens` is 5/7 but +11.5×; `ackermann` is 3/7 at +1.4×.

**<sup>a</sup> Algorithmic asymmetry, against Brood.** `primes`: most languages hoist a `sqrt`
bound where Brood/Clojure re-test `(* d d) > m` each step. `strings`: Brood/Elixir join the
range directly.

**`mandelbrot`: the port drifted twice, and neither was the runtime.** Brood's `/` became
*exact* (a rational, not a float) when kernel rationals landed, so the port's per-pixel
`(/ px n)` on two integers built and discarded 291,600 exact rationals before converting each
to a float anyway — strictly more work than the other six ports do, for an identical checksum,
and worth 192 → 668 ms. Converting to float first (Clojure's `(double py)`, .NET's
`(double)py`, Ruby's `.to_f`; Python/Node/Elixir divide in floats by definition) recovered most
of it. The rest was a second asymmetry the first fix exposed: this port recomputed `y0` for
every *pixel*, where every other port hoists it out of the px loop, so it paid two `->float`
calls per pixel — 583,200 of them, and `->float` is a Brood function call where `(double)` is a
machine cast. Hoisting it restored the row to **192 ms**, its pre-rationals figure.

**There was no runtime regression at any point**, which is worth stating because the
intermediate number looked exactly like one: with *identical* source, the pre-rationals binary
and the current one measure 201 ms and 200 ms.

**<sup>c</sup> Clojure runs cold.** The JVM cold-starts (~0.34 s) on every single-shot run and
HotSpot never fully JIT-compiles the hot loops in that window — a long-running Clojure service
would be far faster than every number in its column.

**<sup>p</sup> Precompiled.** Elixir and .NET are built once and run as compiled artifacts, so
per-run compilation never leaks into their compute. Brood, Clojure, Python, Node and Ruby run
from source each run. This favours Elixir and .NET, and is the fair analog of `node app.js`.

### Immutable structures vs mutable buffers

These five rows are two different comparisons wearing one name. Brood, Elixir and Clojure use
**persistent** structures — every update yields a new value and the old one stays valid.
Python, Node, Ruby and .NET mutate one buffer in place.

**Brood has no mutable data at all** — no `set-car!`, no `vector-set!`, no transients
(ADR-026); the sole exception is `Table`, an opaque store that deep-copies in and out, used by
`sieve` for want of a mutable array.

`sort` lives here rather than in like-for-like: the three persistent languages sort a linked
list into a new one, the four in-place ones sort a flat array. Memory splits on exactly that
line (124–191 MB vs 25–67 MB), so in the other table it read as a Brood memory defect instead
of the price of the guarantee.

**Brood against its actual peers** — the three languages that make the same guarantee:

Here Brood has no peer group, and that *is* the result: it runs its own `std/` codecs written
in Brood, while every other column calls a C, JVM or .NET native implementation. The row
measures the library, not the VM. Sizes are small precisely because Brood is slow here, so the
native columns finish in single-digit ms and the ordering *among them* is meaningless.

**<sup>n</sup> Denominator at the noise floor.** Read Brood's absolute number, not the ratio.
This is the one ordered table with **no `vs best` column**, deliberately: a rating here would be
Brood-in-Brood against a C/JVM/.NET library — 6.7× and 17.9× say nothing about the VM, and the
whole point of the note below is that the denominator is unreliable.
This run shows the failure mode concretely: Elixir's `json` cell is `&lt;1ms`, because
`compute = wall − startup` and its `json` wall (188.9 ms) landed 0.5 ms above its own boot
floor (188.4 ms). Its real JSON time is a few ms; the subtraction, not the runtime, produced
that cell.

### Concurrency — only two of these are the same thing

Brood and Elixir run **preemptively-scheduled isolated processes with copying sends**: a
receiver cannot observe the sender's later mutations, and no unit can starve another. Everything
else here is coroutines on an event loop, OS threads, promises or tasks — cheaper because they
provide less, not because they are better at the same thing.

Against its actual peer:

Brood is never last above; it **is** last on `spawn-live`, below. The field drifts ±10%
run-to-run, so read orderings, not digits. (`spawn-live`, `supervisor` and `latency` are outside
the field-wide aggregate: subset of languages, and `latency` is percentiles.)

**`supervisor` runs two languages and the absence is the point.** An OTP-style supervisor — links
its children, is told when one exits, restarts per a strategy and an intensity budget — exists as
a *runtime* facility only in Brood and Elixir. Elsewhere it would be a loop this repo wrote, which
measures the harness author.

**Moved this run: `spawn-live`** 2.13 → **1.93 s** (−9%), 6.24 → **5.55 CPU·s** (−11%), with RSS
flat at **1.57 GB**. The rule on this row is to disbelieve a table movement until a fixed-baseline
A/B agrees, because it has drifted ~20% between invocations three times. Here the A/B was run
*before* the harness rather than after: the change is `fold` walking a vector by index instead of
coercing through `seq` and `first`/`rest`, where `(rest v)` on a vector materialises a list of the
tail — 15 cons cells and ~48 one-arg primitive dispatches to sum a 16-element payload. Measured at
the time: allocations per unit 27.7 → 15.0, one-arg dispatches 48 → 1.1, and −9% CPU on this row
predicted against −11% observed. Other commits landed in the same window (a std-wide privacy
refactor, test-harness fixes), so the attribution is by prior A/B and mechanism rather than by
bisecting this table; the direction and size agree, and the residual is the row's usual invocation
drift.

The run before it took `spawn-live` 2.56 → 2.13 s (−16% wall, −26% CPU), also A/B-corroborated
(−12.5% wall, −25% CPU): every spawned process had been recompiling the same code — 100,154
bytecode compiles per 100,000 units, because the shared cache was keyed by the closure instance and
a no-capture closure is promoted afresh per creation. Keyed by AST: 163 (brood ADR-215). That
change also took `latency`'s p99.9 658 → 461 µs, since compilation on the arrival path is what an
open-loop tail measures.

`latency` gave some of that back this run — p99 68 → **75 µs**, p99.9 461 → **488 µs** — on a
runtime whose message path did not change. Percentile tails on a 20k req/s open-loop row move by
more than this between invocations, so it is read as drift, not regression; the p99 ranking (2nd of
five, still multiples ahead of third) is unchanged.

Base RSS is **22.1 MB**, flat against the previous run's 22.4 and still up from 18.6 MB before it
(~2 MB with new crypto dependencies, ~1 MB in the ADR-215 commit — not its shared cache, whose
off-switch accounts for ~40 kB). Still undiagnosed.

**From the run before: the `supervisor` row.** Every other row was
within ±3% of the run preceding it. Two apparent swings there were drift, not results, and the
controlled A/B against that commit said so: `spawn-live` read **+20%** in the table and
**−0.0%** under A/B; `pingpong` read +6% and **+1.4%**. That was the third time `spawn-live` had
wandered ~20% between whole harness invocations, which is where this document's rule comes from —
**treat any movement on it as unproven until a fixed-baseline A/B agrees.** The rule earned its
keep in both directions: it has rejected two such swings and confirmed two (see above), which is
the difference between a measurement and a hope. (`reduce` showed −29% then, on
a 3 ms row: the startup subtraction, not the runtime.)

The `supervisor` row is new, so it has no previous number to move from — but it is worth
recording what it would have published at. Measured on the code this suite ran against
yesterday, the same row takes ~5 s at N=20,000 (≈20× Elixir) rather than 818 ms (3.3×). Three
compounding quadratics in the supervised-child path were removed upstream on 2026-07-30: the
supervisor's child list became a pid-keyed map (`start-child` was an O(N) list copy per child,
so N children cost O(N²)), its restart-intensity window became an amortized-O(1) queue (it
re-filtered every retained timestamp on every restart), and a closure that is already shared
code now crosses a local send by handle instead of having its body deep-copied into the
receiver. See the brood repo's devlog and ADR-194.

**Brood vs Elixir** — its closest peer, and the only other language here with both persistent
structures and isolated preemptive processes, so it is the one column that is a like-for-like
comparison end to end. Brood leads the like-for-like core on most rows, and leads its immutable
peers on `wordcount`, `persistent-map` and `sieve`. Elixir leads the latency rows (`pingpong`
62 vs 207 ms, `ring` 268 vs 731 ms — ~2.7–3.3×), **`supervisor` (258 vs 862 ms — 3.3×)**,
`ackermann`, `bintree`, `nqueens`, and the text rows where it uses native codecs. `nbody` is
now close (142 vs 175 ms) where it was 2.2× apart.

**The three remaining process-side gaps are one family, and it is not "per-message cost".**
That was the previous reading of `pingpong`, `ring` and `supervisor`, and profiling on
2026-08-02 contradicted it: measured directly in Brood, a `send` + `receive` costs **1.1 µs**
and a full round trip **4.3 µs** — nowhere near the tens of microseconds those rows imply. What
`latency` was actually paying was the interval between `spawn` and the handler's first
instruction, which is scheduling, and fixing that moved p50 27 → 16 µs without touching the
message path at all. The remaining Elixir gap on these rows is still open, but it should be
re-derived rather than attributed to messaging by assumption.

The mailbox-backlog cliff that used to sit under this is **closed**: a `receive` pinned on a
fresh `ref` now starts its scan past every message that predates the ref, so request/reply is
O(1) in the backlog rather than O(backlog) — 4 µs against 262 µs at a 32,000-message backlog
(ADR-195). It cost `pingpong` and `ring` ~2–3%, which those rows pay without seeing the
benefit because they run with near-empty mailboxes.

## `latency` — what a server actually feels like

Every other concurrency row is **closed loop** — the generator waits for each reply, so a stall
makes it politely stop sending and never enters the numbers (coordinated omission). This row is
**open loop**: request *i* is scheduled at `start + i × (1s / 20,000)` whether the system keeps up
or not, and latency is measured from that instant, so queueing delay lands in the number. Every
20th request occupies ~500 µs of CPU; the percentiles cover the other 95%. Offered load is 0.5 of
12 cores, so the tail is scheduling, not saturation.

<!-- BEGIN LATENCY (generated by bench/docs.py) -->
| | p50 | **p99** | p99.9 | max | cores | CPU·s | peak RSS | vs best (p99) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Elixir** | 8 µs | **56 µs** | 83 µs | 146 µs | 1.7× | 4.60 | 82 MB | −1.3× |
| **Brood** | 18 µs | **75 µs** | 488 µs | 4,286 µs | 1.8× | 4.68 | 121 MB | +1.3× |
| **Node** | 0 µs | **416 µs** | 471 µs | 630 µs | 1.0× | 2.55 | 62 MB | +7.4× |
| **Python** | 31 µs | **506 µs** | 641 µs | 793 µs | 1.0× | 2.52 | 11 MB | +9.0× |
| **.NET** | 4 µs | **871 µs** | 13,191 µs | 15,587 µs | 2.5× | 6.37 | 49 MB | +15.6× |
<!-- END LATENCY -->

**.NET has the best median and the worst tail by 20×** — p50 4 µs, p99.9 12.8 ms, a 3,196×
spread against Elixir's 10×, while spending the most CPU of any port. "Fast in benchmarks, janky
in production" is what that profile looks like, and no other row here can see it.

**Node and Python, single-threaded, tail better than .NET on twelve cores.** Their p99 (~470 µs)
*is* the fat request's own duration: you wait behind exactly one handler, and it stops there.

**Elixir is what the BEAM claims to be** — 8 / 56 / 80 µs: reduction-counted preemption stops a
500 µs handler holding a scheduler, and per-process heaps keep a collection local.

**Brood is second, and the tail gave a little back.** p99 68 → **75 µs**, p99.9 461 → **488 µs**,
p50 14 → **18 µs**, max 1.6 → **4.3 ms**, on a runtime whose message path did not change between
the two runs — so this is invocation drift on a percentile row, not a regression, and the ranking
(2nd of five, multiples ahead of third) is unchanged. The *level* is what the previous runs bought:
over four runs p99 439 → 75, within ~19 µs of the BEAM. The first two gains were scheduler
placement; the third was ADR-215 removing ~8 µs of compilation from every process's *arrival* path
— **a tail can be dominated by one-off setup that throughput rows amortise away.**

The scheduler side: children spawn onto the spawner's own worker, so a dispatcher that keeps
running parks every handler behind it for a quantum. An idle worker now learns immediately that a
peer queued a child (it used to re-probe on a 10 ms timer), with brief first refusal for the owner
so a spawn-then-block parent keeps its child on a warm cache. The remaining gap to Elixir is the
median, and it is **not** per-message cost — a send + receive is 1.1 µs measured directly.

**What this row does not claim.** Handlers are CPU-bound, the hard case; a production Node or
Python service would offload that work. It measures runtimes, not frameworks — no HTTP server, no
router, no serialization. "sustained" confirms every port held the 20,000/s schedule
(19,924–20,000/s), and each calibrates its own fat request to ~500 µs and reports what it achieved
(494–526 µs), so a mis-calibration is visible rather than silent.

## `spawn-live` — 300,000 units held alive, each sent a copied message

Holds **300,000 concurrent units alive at once**, then wakes each individually with a
message it must **copy**, and collects each reply through a queue the parent drains one at a
time. Both halves matter: on the BEAM and in Brood `send` copies, so a receiver cannot
observe the sender's later mutations, and the reply is a *message*, not a return value.

**Only two of the five runtimes here provide the same thing**, so the peer comparison comes
first and the rest is context — the same split the concurrency rows use above.

### Against the only other runtime with the same guarantees

<!-- BEGIN PEER (generated by bench/docs.py) -->
| | compute | peak RSS | cores | CPU·s | vs best |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Elixir** (BEAM process) | 699 ms | 917 MB | 2.3× | 2.02 | −2.8× |
| **Brood** (green process) | 1.93 s | 1.57 GB | 2.9× | 5.55 | +2.8× |
<!-- END PEER -->

**Still Brood's worst row: 2.8× slower and 1.75× heavier than the BEAM.** It has now moved twice
running — this run from `fold` walking a vector by index instead of materialising `(rest v)` as a
list, and the run before because the note here then — "compiled code is shared per runtime" — was
true of the mechanism and false in practice: keyed by the closure *instance*, so this row's 300k
`spawn` thunks and 300k `receive` matchers each compiled their own copy (ADR-215).

What's left is the process itself — mailbox, isolated heap, captured continuation — plus the
**receive machinery**, which a 2026-08-06 decomposition made the largest identified item. An
earlier note here named *per-process inline caches* instead; that was measured and withdrawn — on
the VM a cached callee resolves no faster than an uncached one, so the IC is worth ~2 µs of a 33 µs
unit, not the top item. What the decomposition found instead: a `receive` whose pattern compares a
literal — `[:go v]`, i.e. essentially every real one — generates a matcher that never reaches the
JIT's native fast frame, so each candidate message pays the interpreter's call trampoline. The
structurally identical bind-only pattern `[a v]` does reach it and runs 28% faster.
`(hibernate)` returns most of a process's memory explicitly. See [FRONTIER.md](FRONTIER.md).

### The coroutine runtimes, for context

A promise, an `asyncio` task and a .NET `Task` are closures on a **shared** heap: no isolated
heap, no mailbox, and nothing to preempt. They are cheap because they provide less, not
because they are better at the same thing.

<!-- BEGIN COROUTINE (generated by bench/docs.py) -->
| | compute | peak RSS | cores | CPU·s | vs best |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Node** (promise) | 228 ms | 250 MB | 2.2× | 0.55 | −1.2× |
| **.NET** (`Task`) | 282 ms | 138 MB | 1.6× | 0.49 | +1.2× |
| **Python** (`asyncio` task) | 1.28 s | 362 MB | 1.0× | 1.28 | +5.6× |
<!-- END COROUTINE -->

Two defects here were fixed on 2026-07-30 and the result surprised: .NET's
`TaskCompletionSource` resumed inline on the setter's thread (1000 of 1000, none on the pool), so
"wake 300k units" was 300k synchronous calls; and all three collected results into a pre-allocated
array rather than paying for a second copied message. Forcing .NET to schedule made it *faster*
(345 → 294 ms), so the credit these runtimes get is largely earned — what they do not provide is
structural, priced by the guarantees above rather than the clock. Python still runs at **1.0
cores**: it holds 300k units by never running two.

### The isolated primitive, where each runtime has one

Each runtime's *isolated* primitive does not reach this scale, so it was measured small and
projected: Node's `worker_thread` is linear at ~11.4 MB / ~5.3 ms per unit → **~3.4 TB** at 300k;
Ruby's threads are ~21 KB each but quadratic in time (1.26 s at 5k, 20.78 s at 20k) → **over an
hour**.

**The payload is a contiguous sequence in every port** (a Brood vector, a BEAM tuple, arrays
elsewhere). It was a 16-element cons list in Brood and Elixir until 2026-07-30, which charged the
two process runtimes 16 pointer-chased copies for the same 16 integers.

Measured under the harness, Brood only: **2.53 s / 1693 MB with the vector against 2.85 s /
1703 MB with the list — 11% faster and 0.6% lighter.** (An earlier single-run pair suggested
21% and 33%; it was a sampling artifact and is corrected here.) The split is the interesting
part: representation moved *time* and left *memory* untouched, which says the GB is not the
messages at all — it is the process floor (~5.4 KB × 300,000; sharing the compiled code took the
row's peak RSS 1.75 → 1.58 GB in the 2026-08-05 run, and it has sat flat at ~1.57 GB since).

## Memory (peak RSS) and startup

- **Base RSS**: Brood **22.1 MB**, 3rd-lightest behind Python (9.8) and Ruby (19.3) — the
  lightest of the compiled-class runtimes, though the Ruby gap flips run to run. Brood stays light
  across the suite; the exceptions are the allocation-heavy rows (`sort` 194 MB, `supervisor`
  444 MB, `spawn-live` 1.6 GB). **It went the wrong way two runs ago — 18.6 → 22.4 MB** across
  three brood changes (~2 MB with new crypto dependencies, ~1 MB in the ADR-215 commit — not its
  shared cache, whose off-switch accounts for ~40 kB) — and has sat there since. Undiagnosed.
- **Startup**: Brood ~18 ms, 2nd behind Python (10 ms); Node 18, .NET 22, Ruby 39, Elixir 187,
  Clojure 340. Brood and Node are within a millisecond of each other and trade places run to run.

Both are the warm steady state: Brood's build-id-keyed boot cache costs ~50 ms and ~28 MB on the
first run of a fresh binary, which the harness's warmup keeps out of both columns.

## How to read it

- **Aggregate single-threaded compute** (the chart's x-axis, Σ wall−startup over the core rows,
  normalised): .NET 1.0× · Node 2.8× · **Brood 2.9×** · Elixir 3.5× · Clojure 8.2× · Ruby 12.0× ·
  Python 29.4×. Brood is 3rd of seven; it wobbles ±0.3 run-to-run, so the ordering is the claim.
  It says nothing about behaviour under load — that is what `latency` is for.
- **A single harness sample cannot separate a result from drift.** `spawn-live`'s last two moves
  are real — −16% (A/B: −12.5% wall / −25% CPU) and −9% this run, each with a counted cause; two
  earlier swings on the same row, `spawn` +20% and `spawn-live` −22%, measured −3.6% and −2.0%
  under A/B and were not. Same row, same magnitude, opposite verdicts: only the A/B tells them
  apart.
- **`nbody` 6/7 → 4/7, 323 → 175 ms** two runs back and holding: the JIT types an arm's
  *parameters* only, so a function whose floats arrive from a `def`'d constant lowered its float
  multiply onto the integer path and deopted every activation until the sixteen-deopt rule bailed
  it to the interpreter. Self-healing hid it — a deopt storm became silent interpretation.
- **Where Brood is weakest**: `json`/`regex`/`base64` (in-language codecs against native ones),
  `pipeline` (lazy-seq churn the JIT doesn't cover) and `bintree` (~77 ns/node over four non-tail
  calls — the open watch-item).

The per-language source for every benchmark lives under [`bench/`](bench/), seven files per
benchmark named identically except the extension, so the implementations diff side by side. Run
the suite with `python3 bench/harness.py` (see the [README](README.md#running-it) for options).
